vignette:
Amara's Story

Amara was twenty-three when she arrived in South Sudan as a volunteer nurse with an international medical NGO. She had grown up in Lagos, moved to the United States for university, and carried with her a clear sense of purpose: she would use her training to help people in places where the need was most acute. The clinic where she worked sat on the outskirts of a town that had seen intermittent violence but was, by the standards of the region, relatively stable. She shared a compound with four other expatriate staff and two local nurses. The work was hard and the hours were long, but Amara felt, for the first time in her life, that she was doing something that mattered.

On the afternoon of March 14th, armed men entered the clinic. There was no warning. One moment Amara was changing a dressing on a child's infected wound; the next, she heard shouting in Arabic and gunfire that seemed to come from everywhere at once. She dropped to the floor behind a supply cabinet. A nurse beside her—Aisha, a woman Amara had trained with for six weeks—was struck in the shoulder. Amara watched her collapse. She wanted to move, to help, but her body would not obey. The gunfire continued for what felt like hours but was probably minutes. When it stopped, Amara remained frozen, her hands shaking so violently she could not grip anything. Aisha was bleeding heavily. Amara crawled toward her, finally, but by then armed men were moving through the clinic, and she heard them speaking, heard boots on the tile floor. She pressed herself against the wall and did not move again until soldiers arrived and the men fled.

Aisha survived. Amara was evacuated two days later.

That was two years ago. Since then, Amara has been living in Boston with her boyfriend, Marcus, and working as a nurse in a busy urban hospital. On the surface, she has rebuilt her life. She completed her contract remotely, returned to work, and has maintained her relationship. But the woman who came home from South Sudan is not the woman who left.

The memories come without warning and with a quality of absolute presence. When she recalls the moment she heard the first shots, her heart races as though the gunfire is happening now, in the hospital corridor or in her apartment. She has learned that if she allows herself to fully remember—to see Aisha's face, to feel the weight of her own paralysis—the emotion that floods through her is so overwhelming that she must stop whatever she is doing. She will excuse herself from a patient's room, go to the bathroom, and sit on the toilet with her eyes closed until the wave passes. Sometimes it takes ten minutes. Sometimes longer. On those days, she feels wrung out, depleted by a grief so profound and so specific that she cannot name its object. Is she grieving for Aisha? For the person she was before? For the children in the clinic she did not help?

What frightens Amara most is not the memory itself but what it reveals about her. When she recalls the gunfire, she is forced to confront the fact that she did nothing. She lay behind a cabinet while Aisha bled. She tells herself, rationally, that she was in shock, that there was nothing she could have done, but these explanations feel hollow. She has come to believe that she is fundamentally inadequate—that a truly good nurse, a truly brave person, would have acted. There is something broken in her, something that was exposed that day and cannot be repaired. She feels permanently humiliated by her own cowardice, as though everyone who knows her would recognize this defect if they truly understood what happened.

To manage this, Amara has developed habits that feel, in the moment, like survival. She does not talk about what happened. When Marcus asks, gently, if she wants to discuss her time in South Sudan, she changes the subject. She does not allow herself to think about it directly; instead, when memories begin to surface, she deliberately shifts her attention elsewhere—she focuses intensely on a task at work, or she drifts into a kind of daydream where she imagines herself somewhere else entirely, someone else entirely. These strategies work, in a way. They keep her functional. They allow her to get through her shifts.

But the cost has accumulated slowly. Marcus has stopped asking about her experience. He has also stopped asking about her day, her feelings, or anything that might open a door to difficult conversation. Their intimacy has narrowed. At work, Amara has begun to avoid certain situations—she finds reasons not to work in the trauma bay, where the chaos and urgency can trigger a sense of helplessness that feels too close to that afternoon in the clinic. Her supervisor has noticed that she is less flexible with her scheduling, more rigid in her preferences. She has not been promoted, and she knows, though no one has said it explicitly, that her colleagues see her as less committed than she once was.

Three weeks ago, during a routine shift, a patient came in with a gunshot wound. As Amara approached the bed, something in the sound of the monitors or the urgency in the room transported her completely back to March 14th. She froze. A colleague had to take over. That night, Marcus found her in the bathroom, unable to explain what was wrong. She sat on the edge of the tub and finally told him some of what happened—not all of it, but enough that he understood something was seriously wrong.

He encouraged her to seek help. Amara has made an appointment with a trauma therapist, though she is terrified of what might happen if she actually speaks about that day out loud. She is most afraid that saying the words will make the shame permanent, will confirm what she already believes: that she is broken, that she failed, that there is something fundamentally wrong with her as a person. But she is also beginning to hope that perhaps, with help, she might stop running from her own mind.
